stops.name: Berkeley, the birth at Alta Bates
stops.date_confidence: Date and city attested (Wikipedia; Computer History Museum profile). The hospital is a reconstruction: no source names a birthplace within Berkeley, and Alta Bates on Ashby Avenue is the city's principal maternity hospital of the period. The pin is 2450 Ashby Avenue, replacing a coordinate about 430 metres east that circulates in the research material.
stops.campa: Ralph Charles Merkle is born in Berkeley on the second of February, 1952, to Theodore Charles Merkle, an aeronautical engineer, and into a household where hard engineering is the ordinary weather. Five years later his father will take charge of Project Pluto at Livermore, the attempt to build a nuclear ramjet that stays airborne for months and poisons the ground beneath its flight path. The son will spend his life on two problems that generation posed and did not solve: how strangers can trust each other without meeting, and how matter can be made to build itself.
suggested_refs: Alta Bates Medical Center, 2450 Ashby Avenue, Berkeley, as the city's maternity hospital of the early 1950s
sources: Computer History Museum, Fellow profile of Ralph Merkle

stops.name: Livermore, the nuclear ramjet
stops.date_confidence: Theodore Merkle's directorship of Project Pluto is attested and begins in 1957; 1958 is a default within the program's run. No source dates the family's move to Livermore, and the household's presence there is inferred from Ralph Merkle's later schooling in the town.
stops.campa: Theodore Merkle directs Project Pluto from the Livermore laboratory. The device is a nuclear reactor small enough to ride inside a cruise missile and hot enough to hold it airborne for weeks; the men building it cannot say at dinner what they did all day. The son grows up inside that classification. In this valley a father's work is the part of the day he does not describe, and a program is scheduled in decades. Pluto is cancelled and never flies. In Livermore it still counts as a thing worth having tried to build.

stops.name: Livermore High School, the diploma
stops.date_confidence: Graduation year 1970 attested by Merkle's own curriculum vitae; the month is a default for commencement. A 1963 start date given in earlier material is an unsourced inference, and a four-year attendance from 1966 is the ordinary assumption and equally unattested. stops.campa: He finishes at Livermore High School in 1970, a public school in a laboratory town, and goes over the hills to Berkeley. The sources that later reconstruct his life find nothing to say about these years except the diploma; no anecdote of precocity survives. The field he will overturn does not exist in any university catalogue. Cryptography in 1970 is a government trade practiced behind fences at Fort Meade, and a student who wanted to study it would find no professor in the country willing to teach him.

stops.name: Sather Gate, the university entered
stops.date_confidence: Matriculation year attested by the Computer History Museum profile; the month is a default for the academic calendar. Sather Gate serves as the campus-entrance pin and is not a claim about a particular building.
stops.campa: Merkle passes under Sather Gate as an undergraduate in computer science. Across the bay at Stanford, Martin Hellman is a young assistant professor being told by everyone he respects that cryptography is a dead subject, owned by an agency with a thirty-year head start and an unlimited budget, and that no academic career survives it. Neither man knows the other exists. The problem that will introduce them has not yet been stated by anybody: how two strangers who have never met can agree on a secret in public.

stops.name: Berkeley, the bachelor's degree
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Wikipedia; Computer History Museum); the month is a default for commencement. This is the atlas's canonical Berkeley pin, inherited byte-identical from hellman.journey.json.
stops.campa: He takes his BA in computer science in the spring of 1974 and stays on. That autumn he enrolls in CS 244, Computer Security, taught by Lance Hoffman. Every student in the class is asked for a term-paper proposal, a page or two naming a topic and a plan of work. Merkle hands in seven pages arguing that two people who have never met, watched throughout by an enemy who hears every word, can nevertheless end the conversation holding a secret the enemy does not have.

sources: Ralph Merkle, 'History of Public Key Cryptography,' ralphmerkle.com/1974/

stops.name: Evans Hall, the seven pages for CS 244
stops.date_confidence: The course, the term and the instructor are attested by Merkle's own account and by the scanned proposal at ralphmerkle.com/1974/. The building is a reconstruction: no source places CS 244 in Evans Hall, and the pin follows only from Evans housing Berkeley computer science in the period. The month is a default within Fall 1974.
stops.campa: The proposal sets out Method 1 and Method 2 across seven pages. Hoffman reads it and does not want it. The writing is unclear, and the problem it sets out to solve is not one the field has posed. Merkle does not argue the grade. He drops the course and keeps the idea. Three more refusals follow within three years, from Hoffman again, from an anonymous referee and from an editor, and he answers each the same way, by cutting the argument shorter and sending it back.
stops.quote: Topic: Establishing secure communications between seperate secure sites over insecure communication lines
stops.quote_source: Ralph Merkle, first C.S. 244 project proposal, UC Berkeley, Fall 1974 (FirstCS244projectProposal.pdf, ralphmerkle.com/1974/); spelling as in the original
suggested_refs: The scanned first CS 244 project proposal, seven pages, Merkle's own site
sources: Ralph Merkle, 'History of Public Key Cryptography'

stops.name: Berkeley, the two pages resubmitted
stops.date_confidence: The resubmission is attested by Merkle's own page and by the scanned second proposal; the month is a default within the same term. The instructor's marginal comment is in red pen and reads, as scanned, without the words that some retellings add to it.
stops.campa: He cuts the seven pages to two, strips out the machinery, and states the claim flat at the top of the page. Hoffman writes across it in red: It's getting there, but not good enough yet, see comments. The comment survives, scanned, on Merkle's own website half a century later, filed beside the rejection letters that follow it. He has now been told twice, by a working professional in the field, that the most important idea in modern cryptography is not clear enough to serve as a term paper.
stops.quote: It might seem intuitively obvious that if two people have never had the opportunity to prearrange an encryption method, then they will be unable to communicate securely over an insecure channel. While this might seem intuitively obvious, I believe it is false. I believe that it is possible for two people to communicate securely without having made any prior arrangements that are not completely public.
stops.quote_source: Ralph Merkle, second (two-page, simplified) C.S. 244 project proposal, UC Berkeley, Fall 1974, resubmitted to Lance Hoffman (SecondCS244projectProposal.pdf, ralphmerkle.com/1974/)
suggested_refs: The scanned second CS 244 proposal carrying Lance Hoffman's red-pen comment

stops.name: Berkeley, the third fool

stops.campa: Word crosses the bay. Martin Hellman, hunting the same problem at Stanford and finding almost nobody else in the country working in the open, learns that a student at Berkeley has reached key distribution from a different direction. Hellman's own journey records the phrase he uses: another fool crazy enough to work in the area. Whitfield Diffie, who drove across the country reading declassified archives to arrive at the same question, is already in Hellman's office. Not one of the three has yet published a line on any of it.

stops.name: Berkeley, the paper sent to Susan Graham
stops.date_confidence: Attested to August 1975 by Merkle's own chronology; the day is a default. Susan Graham is a Berkeley professor and an editor of Communications of the ACM, so the pin is the campus rather than a journal office.
stops.campa: He writes the idea up properly and submits it to Susan Graham at Communications of the ACM. The paper opens on the oldest problem in the subject and then does what no published paper has done: it lets two strangers build a shared secret in the open, in front of an eavesdropper, using nothing but puzzles that are cheap to make and expensive to break. The submission is logged in August 1975. That date, and not the date of printing, is what will later settle who arrived first.
stops.quote: People have been communicating with each other for many millennia. They often wish to communicate secretly.
stops.quote_source: Ralph C. Merkle, 'Secure Communications Over Insecure Channels,' Communications of the ACM 21:4 (April 1978), p. 295, opening of the Introduction
suggested_refs: The August 1975 submission of 'Secure Communications over Insecure Channels' to CACM
sources: Ralph Merkle, 'History of Public Key Cryptography,' ralphmerkle.com/1974/

stops.name: Berkeley, the referee's verdict
stops.date_confidence: The date is that of Susan Graham's covering letter, read directly from RejectionLetter.pdf at ralphmerkle.com/1974/; the referee's report is undated and arrives with it. The referee is anonymous in the document and remains unidentified.
stops.campa: The referee is described as an experienced cryptography expert, which in 1975 means a man trained inside the closed world, and his objection is exactly that: experience shows it is extremely dangerous to transmit key information in the clear. The editor adds an objection of her own, that the paper cites no literature. There is no literature. The field this paper belongs to will be founded by it and by one other, and neither is in print yet. Merkle keeps both letters.
stops.quote: I am sorry to have to inform you that the paper is not in the main stream of present cryptography thinking and I would not recommend that it be published in the Communications of the ACM.
stops.quote_source: Anonymous referee, report to Susan L. Graham on Merkle's manuscript 'Secure Communications over Insecure Channels' (ExpertLetter.pdf, ralphmerkle.com/1974/)
suggested_refs: ExpertLetter.pdf and RejectionLetter.pdf, the 1975 CACM referee report and editor's letter

stops.name: Berkeley, the revision of December
stops.date_confidence: Merkle's own chronology dates a revised version to 7 December 1975. The eventual publication carries the original 1975 submission date, which is precisely what the persistence is for.
stops.campa: He revises and sends it back. Graham has asked what stops an eavesdropper from setting N codebreakers on N puzzles in parallel, which is a real question, and the paper answers it; the delay is not purely obstruction, and the argument gets stronger. But nearly three years will pass between the first submission and the printed page, and inside that interval two other men publish the same continent of ideas in a journal that moves faster. He does not withdraw. He waits for the date to be printed.
stops.quote: I persisted for the simple reason that (a) the idea was sound, so CACM would eventually have to concede this fact and publish the article and (b) they would then have to include the original submission date.
stops.quote_source: Ralph Merkle, 'History of Public Key Cryptography,' ralphmerkle.com/1974/

stops.name: Stanford, brought across the bay
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction left standing. One biography puts Merkle's summer with the Diffie and Hellman group in 1976, with the doctorate under Hellman beginning that autumn; the atlas's own hellman.journey.json and diffie.journey.json both date his arrival to June 1975, alongside Diffie's enrolment. Month and day defaulted. Pin is the atlas's canonical Stanford station, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: Hellman brings him across the bay: a summer in the group, then a doctorate under Hellman. For the first time the three of them are in one room. Diffie has the exponential insight, Hellman the analytic discipline, Merkle the puzzles, and between them they constitute very nearly the whole of open cryptography in the United States. Merkle brings the puzzles and something harder to name. The thing everyone said could not be done had already been done, roughly, in a proposal written for a class.
stops.quote: We define a puzzle as a cryptogram which is meant to be broken. To solve the puzzle, we must cryptanalyze the cryptogram.
stops.quote_source: Ralph C. Merkle, 'Secure Communications Over Insecure Channels,' Communications of the ACM 21:4 (April 1978), p. 296, section 'The Method'

stops.name: Stanford, New Directions in Cryptography
stops.date_confidence: Issue month attested; the day is a default. The paper credits Merkle's independently developed puzzle scheme as related work, at a moment when his own account of it is unpublished and sixteen months into the CACM delay.
stops.campa: Diffie and Hellman publish New Directions in Cryptography in the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, and public-key cryptography enters the open literature. The paper credits Merkle's puzzles. It is the credit of a citation, printed while his own account of the same discovery sits in a reviewer's file in Berkeley. Two names go on the doorplate of the new field, and for twenty-six years the key exchange will be called after them alone. In 2002 Hellman will ask publicly that the third name be added.

stops.name: Stanford, the knapsack
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day are defaults. Pin inherited byte-identical from hellman.journey.json, where this stop carries the same date. The break by Adi Shamir is attested to 1982.
stops.campa: Merkle and Hellman publish Hiding Information and Signatures in Trapdoor Knapsacks: a public-key system built on a subset-sum problem that is easy in one direction and believed hard in the other. It is one of the first two candidates in the world for the thing New Directions had described but not supplied. Adi Shamir breaks it in 1982, four years after publication, and the system is abandoned by everyone who had begun to build on it. The other candidate, RSA, does not break.
stops.quote: The author and Martin Hellman have devised an exponential method (public key cryptosystem). Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman have also proposed a public key cryptosystem. Further research is in progress, and the results have been extremely encouraging.
stops.quote_source: Ralph C. Merkle, 'Secure Communications Over Insecure Channels,' Communications of the ACM 21:4 (April 1978), p. 299, Addenda

stops.name: Stanford, the paper published at last
stops.date_confidence: Publication month attested from the issue itself. The printed paper carries its 1975 submission date, which was the object of the three-year fight. The pin is Stanford, where Merkle is by now a doctoral candidate, not Berkeley, where the paper was written.
stops.campa: Communications of the ACM prints Secure Communications Over Insecure Channels in its April 1978 issue, with the submission date attached. Almost three years have passed. Diffie and Hellman's paper has been in print seventeen months; the paper by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman is a year old. The idea has become a field, and Merkle's account of having reached it first, alone, as a student whose professor would not take it as a term paper, arrives into a literature that already exists because of it.
stops.quote: According to traditional conceptions of cryptographic security, it is necessary to transmit a key, by secret means, before encrypted messages can be sent securely. This paper shows that it is possible to select a key over open communications channels in such a fashion that communications security can be maintained.
stops.quote_source: Ralph C. Merkle, 'Secure Communications Over Insecure Channels,' Communications of the ACM 21:4 (April 1978), p. 294, abstract
suggested_refs: The April 1978 issue of Communications of the ACM, carrying the 1975 submission date

stops.name: Stanford, the doctorate and the tree
stops.date_confidence: Degree conferred 17 June 1979; the dissertation is 'Secrecy, Authentication, and Public Key Systems.' The thesis PDF is self-hosted at ralphmerkle.com and was not found independently mirrored in a library catalogue during this research, which is recorded as a single-copy dependency rather than a doubt about the text.
stops.campa: The thesis is titled Secrecy, Authentication, and Public Key Systems, and buried inside it is a construction he calls tree authentication. Hash the items in pairs, hash the hashes, and again, until one value at the top commits to every leaf beneath it; then any single leaf can be proved to belong by producing a short path instead of the whole set. He is solving a signature problem. He has built the data structure that thirty years later will hold every transaction in every block of a currency he does not invent.
suggested_refs: Merkle, 'Secrecy, Authentication, and Public Key Systems,' Stanford PhD thesis, 1979

stops.campa: Stanford files, as his assignee, the application for a method of providing digital signatures by means of the authentication tree. Two years earlier the same university filed another: US 4,200,770, Cryptographic Apparatus and Method, which names Diffie, Hellman and Merkle together as co-inventors. The founding legal document of public-key cryptography carries all three names, whatever the protocol is called in textbooks. Patents, unlike journals, record the date of filing and do not argue about it.

stops.campa: US Patent 4,309,569, Method of providing digital signatures, issues to Ralph C. Merkle, assigned to Stanford. It describes the hash tree in the flat language of claims. The patent expires in 1999, nine years before an anonymous author builds a currency on the structure it describes and cites Merkle in a list of eight references. Nobody in 1982 is looking for a way to let strangers agree on a ledger without a bank, because nobody has yet noticed that this is the same problem he solved as a student.

Merkle will spend eleven years there. He designs block ciphers and hash functions, publishes on molecular manufacturing, and holds two futures at once: the cryptographic one that has already happened to him, and a second one, in which machines assemble matter atom by atom, that has not yet happened to anybody.

stops.campa: He presents A Certified Digital Signature at Santa Barbara, and inside it the method for building a collision-resistant hash function over inputs of any length out of a fixed-size compression function. Ivan Damgard, working separately, publishes the same construction the same year. The field names it for both men and declines to adjudicate between them, which is the outcome Merkle did not get in 1976. Nearly every hash function in use for the next quarter century is built this way.

stops.date_confidence: The two block ciphers and the hash function are attested to Merkle's PARC period; 1990 is a default within it, and the design work spans several years rather than a single one.
stops.campa: He names two block ciphers and a hash function after pharaohs who built pyramids: Khufu, Khafre, Snefru. The names sit oddly well on a discipline whose central objects are one-way functions, structures cheap to raise in one direction and, by design, ruinous to reverse in the other. He is working now inside an established field with journals, conferences, program committees and a federal standards body. Sixteen years earlier the whole of it was seven pages a professor declined to accept.

stops.name: Palo Alto, information-theoretic death
stops.date_confidence: Publication year 1992, in Medical Hypotheses; month and day are defaults. The pin is the atlas's canonical Palo Alto station, inherited byte-identical from hellman.journey.json, and stands for where he is living and working rather than for a place of publication.
stops.campa: Merkle publishes The Technical Feasibility of Cryonics and coins a term for what he means by dying: information-theoretic death, the point at which the structure encoding a person can no longer be inferred from what remains, by any technology whatever. It is a cryptographer's definition. It moves the boundary of death off the failure of an organ and onto the destruction of a message, and a message that can still be read by any means at all has not been destroyed.

stops.date_confidence: Merkle's own home page gives 'Director, Alcor' from 21 May 1998; a Wikipedia line dating his board membership to 2006 is eight years late and is not followed here. He also serves on Alcor's scientific advisory board, with no start date attested.
stops.campa: He joins the board of directors of Alcor, nine years after signing his own contract with it. The organization keeps a few dozen patients in liquid nitrogen in a warehouse in Arizona, on the argument that the law's definition of death and the physics of information do not agree with one another. He has by now published in cryptography and in molecular manufacturing, and the Alcor argument runs on the same question as both of them: what can in principle be recovered, and by whom.
suggested_refs: Alcor Life Extension Foundation board records, from 21 May 1998

stops.name: Santa Clara, the Feynman Prize
stops.date_confidence: The prize is presented at the banquet of the Sixth Foresight Conference on Molecular Nanotechnology, Westin Hotel, Santa Clara, which ran 13 to 15 November 1998; the 12 November date given in some material is the tutorial day and is corrected here. Which evening within the three days carried the banquet is not fixed.
stops.campa: At the sixth Foresight conference Merkle receives the Feynman Prize in Nanotechnology for theoretical work, an award named for the physicist who told an audience at Caltech in 1959 that there is plenty of room at the bottom and that nothing in physics forbids arranging atoms one at a time. Richard Feynman's lecture was a provocation with no program attached to it. Merkle's citation is for supplying arithmetic: what such machines would have to obey, and what they would cost to run.
suggested_refs: The Sixth Foresight Conference on Molecular Nanotechnology, Westin Hotel, Santa Clara, 13 to 15 November 1998

stops.name: Richardson, Zyvex
stops.date_confidence: Employment from 1999 to 2003 attested by Merkle's curriculum vitae; month and day are defaults. Coordinates are approximate to 1301 North Plano Road, Richardson; a point about three kilometres north, near the Plano line, circulates in the research material and is not used. The IEEE Koji Kobayashi Award falls in this same year with no location attested anywhere reached.
stops.campa: He leaves Xerox PARC after eleven years and moves to Texas, to Zyvex, the first company organized around building a molecular assembler. He leaves the field he founded at the moment it turns into an industry, for one that has produced no product and may never produce one. The same year the IEEE gives him the Koji Kobayashi Award for work he did before he was thirty. The prizes arrive for the first subject while he is already three states away, working on the second.
suggested_refs: Zyvex Corporation, Richardson, Texas, and its molecular assembler program

stops.name: San Jose, the RSA Award for Excellence in Mathematics
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to place. The award and the year are attested; that the presentation took place at that year's RSA Conference in San Jose is a reasonable inference and is not separately confirmed. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: The RSA Conference gives him its award for excellence in mathematics. The company is named for the three men whose cryptosystem was announced in the addendum of Merkle's own delayed paper, and it was built on a concept the Stanford patent attributes to Diffie, Hellman and Merkle jointly. A commercial industry now stands where in 1974 there was a seven-page term-paper proposal and a professor's note in red pen saying that it was getting there but not good enough yet.

stops.name: Palo Alto, the Institute for Molecular Manufacturing
stops.date_confidence: Merkle's curriculum vitae gives the IMM senior research fellowship from 2001, overlapping his Zyvex and Georgia Tech years; a widely repeated 2006 start date, tied to his return to California, is wrong and is corrected here. An IEEE biography places the institute in Cupertino rather than Palo Alto and that disagreement is unresolved. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: He becomes a senior research fellow of the Institute for Molecular Manufacturing while still working in Texas, a fellowship he will keep across every subsequent move. The institute is small, unendowed, and devoted to a technology whose feasibility is still being argued in letters columns. His procedure with an unfinished field has not changed since he was twenty-two. He works out what the thing would have to be if it existed, publishes the arithmetic, and waits for the objections to arrive in writing.
suggested_refs: Institute for Molecular Manufacturing, senior research fellowship from 2001

stops.name: Georgia Institute of Technology, the Distinguished Professorship
stops.date_confidence: Appointment from 2003 to 2006, leading the Georgia Tech Information Security Center, attested by Merkle's curriculum vitae; month and day are defaults. The pin is the College of Computing building on Atlantic Drive; the Klaus Advanced Computing Building, named in earlier material, did not open until 2006 and cannot be where he worked.
stops.campa: Merkle crosses the country again, to Atlanta, as Distinguished Professor and head of the Georgia Tech Information Security Center. He is now teaching and directing in the field he opened as a student who could not get a term paper accepted in it. In 2004 he publishes Kinematic Self-Replicating Machines with Robert Freitas, a survey of every proposal ever made for a machine that builds a copy of itself, which is the nanotechnology problem stated in its hardest available form.
suggested_refs: Georgia Tech Information Security Center, 2003 to 2006; Freitas and Merkle, Kinematic Self-Replicating Machines (2004)

stops.name: Palo Alto, the return west
stops.date_confidence: The return to the San Francisco Bay Area in 2006 is attested; month and day are defaults. Two claims commonly bundled with this move are separated here: the IMM fellowship begins in 2001, and Singularity University does not exist until 2008.
stops.campa: The Georgia appointment ends and he comes back to northern California, where he has spent all but four years of his life, inside a rectangle roughly forty miles on a side containing Berkeley, Stanford, Palo Alto, Mountain View and San Jose. Every institution he has worked for except Zyvex and Georgia Tech stands within it. The whole invention of public cryptography, its patent, its two competing priority claims and its three co-inventors, happened within an hour's drive of where he was born.
suggested_refs: The Bay Area institutions of Merkle's career: Berkeley, Stanford, Elxsi, Xerox PARC, IMM

stops.name: Palo Alto, eight references
stops.date_confidence: The Bitcoin white paper is circulated on 31 October 2008 and carries no place; the pin stands for where Merkle is living, not for an event he attends, and carries no evidential weight. Reference 8 of that paper is R. C. Merkle, 'Protocols for public key cryptosystems,' Proceedings of the 1980 Symposium on Security and Privacy.
stops.campa: An author calling himself Satoshi Nakamoto circulates a nine-page paper describing a currency with no bank inside it. Its reference list has eight entries and one of them is Merkle. The block structure hashes transactions in pairs, then hashes the hashes, and keeps only the root in each header: tree authentication, out of the 1979 thesis, doing the job it was designed to do in a system its author never imagined. Merkle is fifty-six, and hears of it at first the way most people do, which is not at all.
suggested_refs: Satoshi Nakamoto, 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System,' reference 8

stops.name: Moffett Field, Singularity University
stops.date_confidence: Singularity University is founded in September 2008 and formally launched at NASA Ames in February 2009; Merkle joins its faculty in the nanotechnology track and later becomes Chair Emeritus of Nanotechnology. A 2006 date for this appointment, which circulates widely, is impossible and is corrected here. Month and day are defaults. The IACR fellowship is attested to 2008 with no venue.
stops.campa: He joins the faculty of Singularity University on the NASA Ames campus at Moffett Field, teaching nanotechnology in a district of hangars built for airships. He has been named an IACR Fellow the year before. Both subjects he has carried since the 1970s are now respectable enough to be taught: one because it turned out to underwrite all electronic commerce, the other because the argument has never been settled and the people making it have not gone away.

stops.name: San Francisco, the Hamming Medal
stops.date_confidence: The 2010 IEEE Richard W. Hamming Medal to Diffie, Hellman and Merkle is attested; no ceremony is located for it. The 20 August 2011 San Francisco event often cited was the 2011 Honors Ceremony held with the IEEE Sections Congress, and a misleading URL slug on an IEEE video listing appears to be the source of the confusion. This pin is the atlas's canonical San Francisco station and carries no evidential weight; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: The IEEE names Diffie, Hellman and Merkle the 2010 Hamming Medalists, for the invention of public-key cryptography and its application to secure communications. The citation for Merkle runs longer than that phrase: the puzzles, the tree, the signature scheme, the hash construction shared with Damgard. Four separate objects in the foundations of the field carry his name, and the working engineers who use them daily know the name from the objects rather than from the history. The key exchange that started all of it still carries two names.
suggested_refs: IEEE Richard W. Hamming Medal, 2010 citation
sources: Foresight Institute, 'Merkle wins Hamming Medal with Diffie, Hellman'

stops.name: Alexandria, the National Inventors Hall of Fame
stops.date_confidence: The joint induction of Diffie, Hellman and Merkle in 2011 is attested; the class is announced 3 March and the ceremony held 4 May. Contradiction left standing: several sources, including an on-site report, place the ceremony in the old US Patent Office Building in Washington, D.C., at about 38.8977, -77.0219, while diffie.journey.json and hellman.journey.json both pin this stop at Alexandria, Virginia, dated 2011-01-01. The atlas pin is inherited byte-identical here and the documentary venue is recorded in this note.
stops.campa: The three are inducted together into the National Inventors Hall of Fame, for the 1977 patent that names all three. The same stop stands in Diffie's journey and in Hellman's, worded almost identically, which is how the atlas records that this is not three careers that happened to touch but one event with three men inside it. Merkle is fifty-nine. He has spent a decade on machines that build copies of themselves, and is being honored for something he did in a class he dropped.

stops.name: Alfred Lerner Hall, Columbia University, the Levchin Prize
stops.date_confidence: Award year attested; the Real World Crypto Symposium of 2020 was held at Columbia University and the pin is Alfred Lerner Hall. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: At the Real World Crypto Symposium an audience of working engineers gives Merkle the Levchin Prize, for the invention of hash trees and cryptographic hashing. The citation names the structure rather than the protocol, and the room is full of people who use it every day in systems that did not exist when he built it: version control, certificate transparency logs, distributed ledgers, backup deduplication. He is sixty-eight years old. The tree has outrun the puzzles.

stops.name: Scottsdale, the arrangement that stands in for a grave
stops.date_confidence: Status at the time of this research, August 2026; the date is the atlas convention for a living subject. No obituary, grave or memorial exists to record, and none was expected. Whether the Alcor contract is neuro or whole body is not attested in anything checked and is left open.
stops.campa: There is no tomb to visit. Merkle is alive in California, and the only site the atlas can offer in place of a grave is a warehouse in Arizona holding steel dewars of liquid nitrogen, to which he has held a standing contract since 1989. He proposed once that death be defined as the loss of recoverable information rather than the stopping of a heart. The puzzles, the tree and the dewars all run on one question: what survives, in what form, and who can prove it later without having been present.
suggested_refs: Alcor Life Extension Foundation, Scottsdale, as the prospective site of a journey with no tomb
